newsitem.title: INDIA: India money, forex markets seen integrating.
newsitem.headline: India money, forex markets seen integrating.

text.p: Higher Indian call money rates are pushing up forward dollar premiums, reflecting their growing linkage in financial markets, bankers said on Monday.
Call money rates moved up from around eight percent at the beginning of last week to cross 12 percent on Thursday. On Friday, call money was between 10.25 and 10.75 percent.
Premiums on forward dollars firmed in response, with the rates for six-month dollars going up to an annualised 8.77 percent on Friday from around 6.5 percent on Monday last week.
In afternoon trade on Monday, call money was 10.50 percent and premiums on six-month dollars was 8.9 percent, dealers said.

"There are definite signs of call money and foward markets becoming more integrated," said P.H. Ravikumar, senior vice-president at ICICI Banking Corporation. "In particular, short-term forward premiums are closely tracking call money rates."
Bankers said this was in contrast to earlier days when supply and demand were the primary determinants of forward rates.

"The forward rates reflect demand and supply rather than interest rate differentials owing to the absence of integration between the money and forex markets," an expert group constituted by the Reserve Bank of India said in a report on the Indian foreign exchange market in 1995.

The relation between short-term forward premiums and call money rates could also be because of a change in the composition of the market, said the head of treasury at a foreign bank, who declined to be identified.
"In general, the share of exporters and importers in the forward market's turnover is less now," he said, adding that bank treasury operations played a major role in determining forward rates.
"There is no doubt that in the short-term, perceptions on the movement of call money rates are influencing forward premiums," Ravikumar said.

If call money rates were firm and market perceptions were that the trend would continue, banks would resort to a sell-buy swap, selling dollars for the Indian currency to generate rupee funds in the first leg of the transaction.
In the second leg, banks would buy dollars forward, pushing up forward premiums further.
Many of India's state-run banks are planning to integrate their domestic money market and foreign exchange treasury operations, reflecting an awareness of the changing situation.
At present, forex operations and domestic money market operations are independent of each other in these banks. Foreign banks and several private banks have already integrated treasury operations.
Integrating operations would help banks take advantage of arbitrage opportunities between markets, dealers said.
